rows.verified: Employers have a duty to prevent exposure to lead or, where prevention is not reasonably practicable, adequately control it.
Employers should reduce the number of people exposed, the amount of lead exposure and the duration of exposure.
Lead controls should be selected using suitable industry good practice and used whenever required.
Mechanical, administrative and respiratory controls must be maintained in effective working order.
Employers should keep records demonstrating that exposure control is being sustained.
Appropriate medical surveillance should be discussed with an appointed doctor.
Clean and contaminated work clothing should be stored separately and suitable washing facilities provided.
Lead exposure can affect the blood, nervous system, kidneys, blood pressure and reproductive health.
The required control and surveillance depend on lead form, task, route, concentration, duration and individual exposure history.
Lead evidence is substance-, process- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
Work-related skin disease can be caused or worsened by chemicals, wet work and prolonged contact with water.
Dermatitis is the most common work-related skin disease, while urticaria and occupational skin cancer can also occur.
Contact dermatitis may result from irritants or from an allergic reaction to a sensitising substance.
Signs can include redness, scaling, blistering, weeping, cracking and swelling.
Symptoms may include itching and pain and can become severe enough to prevent continued work.
Repeated wet work, soaps, detergents, solvents, oils, acids, alkalis, dust and wet cement can contribute to dermatitis.
Employers and workers can use the Avoid, Protect and Check approach to prevent and detect skin disease.
Regular skin checks can support early identification and treatment of occupational dermatitis.
The correct prevention programme depends on the substance, wet-work duration, glove selection, skin condition, task and worker sensitivity.
Skin-disease evidence is exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
